title: (Scenario) How would you scale a key-value store toward ~1M requests/sec: why is "add more servers" insufficient, and what must you actually specify (how data is partitioned across nodes and how a request is routed to the right node, replication for availability, capacity planning, handling traffic SKEW / hot keys, and what happens when a node fails)?
shortTitle: How would you scale a key-value store toward ~1M requests/sec
keyPoints: Adding servers without a partitioning scheme means the new servers hold no data and receive no traffic.
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes distributes keys evenly and moves only 1/N of data when scaling.
Request routing via a coordinator, smart client, or gossip must stay consistent with the current ring.
Replication factor of 3 with quorum reads/writes (R + W > N) balances consistency and availability.
Capacity planning divides target TPS by per-node throughput, multiplies by replication, and adds headroom for peak.
Hot keys are handled with caching, extra replicas, sub-key sharding, and per-key rate limiting.
Node failures are routine: surviving replicas serve traffic, gossip marks the node down, and hinted handoff catches up.

s1_definition.oneliner: Reaching a million requests per second means specifying partitioning, request routing, replication, capacity planning, hot-key handling, and node-failure behaviour, because adding servers alone does nothing until data is partitioned and requests are routed to the node that owns each key.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Partitioning** – data is divided across nodes using consistent hashing with virtual nodes so each node owns a distinct slice of the keyspace.
- **Routing** – a coordinator, smart client, or gossip-based membership ensures each request reaches the node that owns its key.
- **Replication** – each key is stored on N successive ring nodes for availability and read scaling, with quorum parameters (R + W > N) for consistency.
- **Capacity planning** – target TPS divided by per-node throughput gives the node count, multiplied by the replication factor and headroom for peak.
- **Hot-key handling** – caching, extra replicas, sub-key sharding, and per-key rate limiting prevent one key from overwhelming one node.
- **Node-failure behaviour** – surviving replicas serve traffic, gossip marks the node down, and hinted handoff delivers missed writes on recovery.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must serve a million customer lookups a second. Just hiring more clerks does nothing if every customer still forms one queue at one desk. You must split customers across desks (partitioning), tell each customer which desk is theirs (routing), keep spare copies of each file at other desks (replication), calculate how many desks you need from the expected crowd (capacity planning), and have a plan for a celebrity customer whose desk gets mobbed (hot keys) and for when a desk closes (node failure).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Consistent Hash Ring with Replication (N=3)

        Node-A
       /      \
      /   key  \
  Node-D   SAV2001   Node-B   ← key assigned to Node-B
      \    │  /                  replicated to Node-C, Node-D
       \   ▼ /
        Node-C

  Capacity Planning
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1M req/s ÷ 100K/node = 10 throughput nodes  │
  │ × 3 replicas = 30 storage nodes              │
  │ × 1.5 headroom = 45 nodes in production      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Hot Key Mitigation
  ┌──────────┐    cache hit    ┌───────┐
  │  Client  │ ──────────────► │ Cache │  (most reads)
  │          │                 └───────┘
  │          │    cache miss   ┌───────┐
  │          │ ──────────────► │ Node  │  (rare)
  └──────────┘                 └───────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Scaling a key-value store toward a million requests per second is a distributed-systems design problem, not a matter of adding servers. Extra servers help only if you specify how data is partitioned with consistent hashing, how requests are routed to the owning node, how data is replicated with quorum parameters for consistency and availability, how capacity is planned from a throughput and latency budget, how hot keys are handled through caching and sub-key sharding, and how the system behaves when a node fails.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj built exactly this kind of store for session and balance lookups. When a manager suggested simply adding servers, Pankaj explained that without partitioning and routing those servers do nothing. The team used consistent hashing with virtual nodes, a replication factor of three with quorum reads and writes, and planned the node count from a throughput budget with headroom. The lesson that stuck most was the hot key: one huge merchant account would have melted its node until they fronted it with a cache and per-key rate limiting.

The senior nuances are to separate the control plane from the data plane, pick quorum parameters per use case, put a caching tier in front for read-heavy traffic, and monitor per-node and per-key metrics so skew and failures are caught fast.

Remember one sentence: reaching 1M req/sec means concretely specifying partitioning, routing, replication with quorums, capacity planning with headroom, hot-key mitigation, and node-failure recovery, because adding servers alone does nothing until data is partitioned and requests are routed.
